newsitem.title: ISRAEL: FORECAST-Analysts mixed on Israel interest rates.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Analysts mixed on Israel interest rates.

text.p: Analysts were divided on Sunday on the direction of Israeli interest rates this week, with some predicting a slight reduction of 0.3 percentage point while others forecast no change at all.
The central Bank of Israel will announce on Thursday its monetary programme for May. Its base rate has remained at an annualised 13.9 percent since the end of February.
"There's no room for monetary loosening," said Jonathan Katz, chief economist at Solid Financial Markets.

"The past two months the CPI (consumer price index) has been relatively high, both to the inflation target and to the forecast of the private sector so that even though fiscal figures for the first quarter were better than expected and even though recent M1 figures were also good, with all that said and done the bottom line is the central bank has to be very cautious."
In March the CPI rose by 1.0 percent, against forecasts of a 0.7 percent increase and following a sharp 1.2 percent gain in February.
The government has set a 1997 inflation target of seven to 10 percent while inflation in the past 12 months totalled 10.4 percent.
On the other hand the M1 money supply dropped 1.3 percent in March. "I hear the April M1 is also good," Katz said.

The CPI in April traditionally is high, because of the week-long Jewish holiday of Passover. Katz, who is forecasting a rise of 1.1 percent in April, believes the central bank will await the April CPI before lowering rates, despite a slowdown in the Israeli economy.

Others are more optimistic of a cut. "I think the central bank will lower interest rates by 0.3 percentage point," said financial consultant Eliezer Carmel. "The summer CPIs will be low, rising 0.5 percentage point in May, June and July."
Carmel said the March CPI was above expectations because of the volatile fruit and vegetable and housing components. "The core of inflation is not accellerating," he said.
Gidi Halpern, investment manager at Meitav Investments and Securities, noted that interest rate forecasts fluctuated between no change to a slight reduction.
Halpern said he believes the Treasury is likely to cut the budget by 700 million shekels, giving the central bank room to ease up on interest rates.

However, a budget cut will depend on whether Dan Meridor remains as finance minister, Halpern said. The future of the entire government is uncertain in the wake of a corruption scandal surrounding Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Israel's attorney general is expected to announce later on Sunday whether to charge Netanyahu.

Major Israeli newspapers and radio stations predicted the prime minister would not be indicted. But the reports said he could face a rebellion from cabinet ministers who could topple his coalition government if the findings raised serious questions about his integrity.
"Any interest rate cut will be welcomed by the markets. But that would last for about two hours if on the same day it is announced that Netanyahu is going to jail," Halpern said.
